findings.claim: “Parameters with defaults come after those without” is unqualified. Python permits a required keyword-only parameter after a defaulted positional parameter, for example def f(a=1, *, b). The nearby “every positional argument must come before” wording also has starred-unpacking exceptions.

evidence.section: Function definitions: parameter_list grammar, positional and keyword-only parameters

findings.recommendation: Scope the rule explicitly: among ordinary positional-or-keyword parameters, a required parameter cannot follow a defaulted one; in introductory calls, place unstarred positional arguments before keywords. Avoid claiming these as universal grammar rules.

findings.claim: The page teaches that dict keys “must be immutable” and that “a tuple works.” Python actually requires keys to be hashable; a tuple is hashable only when all its elements are hashable. For example, hash(([1],)) raises TypeError. This matters to the objective of choosing a collection/key.

evidence.section: Hashable definition and immutable-sequence hashability

findings.recommendation: Replace the rule with “dict keys must be hashable.” State that strings, numbers, and tuples containing only hashable values work; lists and tuples containing a list do not. Keep the concrete city-pair quiz answer, whose strings make that tuple hashable.

findings.claim: “Slicing … always returns a new object” is false for immutable sequences. On the required CPython 3.14.6 interpreter, "python"[:] is "python" evaluated True; implementations may reuse immutable objects. List slicing does create a new list.

evidence.section: Common Sequence Operations and immutable sequence types

findings.recommendation: Say that slicing returns a sequence value of the same type; list slices are new lists, while learners must not rely on distinct identity for immutable strings. Retain the correct claim that ordinary out-of-range slice bounds do not raise IndexError.

findings.claim: The single Windows activation command .venv\Scripts\activate is presented as universal and is the keyed GIFT answer, but the official venv table gives different commands by shell: activate.bat for cmd.exe and Activate.ps1 for PowerShell. The current instruction can fail in the shell many Windows learners use.

evidence.section: How venvs work: platform- and shell-specific activation command table

findings.recommendation: Teach and quiz both Windows shells explicitly: .venv\Scripts\activate.bat in cmd.exe and .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1 in PowerShell; keep source .venv/bin/activate for POSIX shells.

findings.claim: The asserted sys.path order—script folder, standard library, site-packages—is too absolute. Initialization can begin with the script directory or current directory, includes PYTHONPATH, prefix-dependent standard-library entries, and then site processing; -m, -c, isolated mode, environment variables, ._pth files, and sitecustomize change the path.

evidence.section: The initialization of the sys.path module search path

findings.recommendation: Label the three-entry diagram as the simplified normal case and add the omitted practical rule: import searches sys.path in order, whose initial entries depend on how Python starts and can be influenced by PYTHONPATH/site configuration. Avoid a universal three-step order in the quiz feedback.
